# autometrics::exemplars - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autometrics/latest/autometrics/exemplars/index.html

**crate features**only.

`exemplars-tracing` or `exemplars-tracing-opentelemetry` or `exemplars-tracing-opentelemetry-0_31`## Expand description

Connect metrics to traces using exemplars.

Exemplars are a newer Prometheus / OpenMetrics / OpenTelemetry feature that allows you to associate specific traces or samples with a given metric. This enables you to investigate what caused metrics to change by looking at individual examples that contributed to the metrics.

Autometrics integrates with tracing libraries to extract details from the current span context and automatically attach them as exemplars to the generated metrics.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-metrics-libraries)Supported metrics libraries

Exemplars are currently only supported with the `prometheus-client` metrics library,
because that is the only one that currently supports producing metrics with exemplars.

[§](https://docs.rs#exposing-metrics-to-prometheus-with-exemplars)Exposing metrics to Prometheus with exemplars

To enable Prometheus to scrape metrics with exemplars you must:

- Run Prometheus with the `--enable-feature=exemplar-storage`
- Export the metrics to Prometheus using the provided `prometheus_exporter::encode_http_response``Content-Type`header to indicate it is using the the OpenMetrics format, rather than the default Prometheus format:

`Content-Type: application/openmetrics-text; version=1.0.0; charset=utf-8`[§](https://docs.rs#tracing-libraries)Tracing libraries

See the [ tracing submodule docs](https://docs.rs/tracing/index.html).

Extract exemplars from the OpenTelemetry Context attached to the current tracing Span.

This works in the following way:

- Add the `tracing_opentelemetry::OpenTelemetryLayer`
- That layer ensures that there is an `opentelemetry::Context``tracing::Span`
- Spans can be manually created or created for every function using the `tracing::instrument`
- Autometrics extracts the `trace_id`and`span_id`from the`Context`and attaches them as exemplars to the generated metrics

See the `exemplars-tracing-opentelemetry` example for usage details.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [tracing](https://docs.rs/tracing/index.html)- `exemplars_tracing`
- Extract fields from `tracing::Span`

# sourceatlas 0.2.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sourceatlas/0.2.3

# SourceAtlas

SourceAtlas is a command-line tool written in Rust that scans a source code repository and generates useful statistics.

I started this project as a way to learn Rust by building something practical instead of only completing exercises. The goal isn't to compete with existing tools, but to build a clean, well-structured application while learning more about idiomatic Rust and software engineering.

## Features

Current features include:

- Recursive directory scanning
- Ignores common build and IDE directories:
- `target`
- `build`
- `node_modules`
- `.idea`
- `.vscode`

- Reports:
- Directories scanned
- Files scanned
- Files analyzed
- Files skipped
- Total lines

- Gracefully skips unreadable or binary files
- Unit tested

## Installation

Install from crates.io:

```
```
Or build from source:

```
```

```

# sidereon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon/0.11.0/sidereon/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#sidereon)sidereon

A thin, ergonomic API over the [ sidereon_core](https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sidereon_core/index.html) engine. It does not model
anything itself: every function here delegates to a

`sidereon_core` reference
entry point and re-exports its result structs, so the numerical behavior is
identical to calling the core directly. The value it adds is a small, human
surface:- `load_sp3`
- `parse_antex`- `load_antex`
- `parse_rinex_nav`- `load_rinex_nav`
- `parse_rinex_obs`- `load_rinex_obs`
- `lint_rinex_obs`- `lint_rinex_nav`- `repair_rinex_obs`- `repair_rinex_nav`
- `parse_rinex_clock`- `load_rinex_clock`
- `decode_crinex`- `load_crinex`
- `solve_spp`
- `solve_velocity`
- `solve_rtk_float_with`- `solve_rtk_fixed_with`
- `solve_ppp_float_with`- `solve_ppp_fixed_with`
- GNSS utility modules such as `frequencies``combinations``quality``carrier_phase``signal``velocity``broadcast_comparison``constants``navigation``geometry``data``dgnss``constellation``ppp_corrections``rtk``staleness``tides``ils``terrain`
- `astro`
- `tle`- `sgp4`- `passes`- `tca`
- one `Error`

The input, result, and ephemeris types each function takes and returns are
re-exported from `sidereon_core` under [ antex](https://docs.rs/antex/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/rinex/index.html)

`rinex`[,](https://docs.rs/astro/index.html)

`astro`[,](https://docs.rs/ephemeris/index.html)

`ephemeris`[,](https://docs.rs/positioning/index.html)

`positioning`[, and the curated](https://docs.rs/observables/index.html)

`observables`[/](https://docs.rs/rtk_filter/index.html)

`rtk_filter`[facades, so a consumer imports the ergonomic API types from this one crate. Lower-level RTK/PPP internals remain available under](https://docs.rs/precise_positioning/index.html)

`precise_positioning`[with their native core errors.](https://docs.rs/raw/index.html)

`raw````
// Malformed input surfaces a single error type.
let parsed = sidereon::load_sp3(b"not a valid sp3 file");
assert!(matches!(parsed, Err(sidereon::Error::Sp3(_))));
```
Lower-level helpers re-exported through modules such as [ rinex](https://docs.rs/rinex/index.html) keep their
native core error type. Map them explicitly at wrapper boundaries; there is
intentionally no blanket conversion into

[.](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)

`Error`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn decode_from_reexported_core() -> sidereon::Result<()> {
    sidereon::rinex::decode_crinex("not a CRINEX file\n")?;
    Ok(())
}
```
Low-level RTK and PPP core modules live behind the explicit [ raw](https://docs.rs/raw/index.html) escape
hatch, not the ergonomic facades.

`let _ = sidereon::raw::rtk_filter::RtkFilterScratch::new();`Hot-path RTK filter APIs are intentionally not part of the ergonomic
`sidereon::rtk_filter` facade.

PPP preparation and raw solver APIs are intentionally not part of the
ergonomic `sidereon::precise_positioning` facade.

RTK config builders consume the config. Dropping the returned value must not leave an unchanged copy available for solving.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use sidereon::{
    rtk_filter::{FloatSolveOpts, MeasModel, StochasticModel},
    RtkFloatConfig,
};
let epochs = Vec::new();
let ambiguity_ids = Vec::<String>::new();
let model = MeasModel {
    code_sigma_m: 0.3,
    phase_sigma_m: 0.003,
    sagnac: true,
    stochastic: StochasticModel::Rtklib,
};
let opts = FloatSolveOpts {
    position_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
    ambiguity_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
    max_iterations: 1,
};
let config = RtkFloatConfig::new(&epochs, [0.0; 3], &ambiguity_ids, &model, opts);
config.with_initial_baseline_m([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]);
let _ = sidereon::solve_rtk_float_with(config);
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use sidereon::{
    rtk_filter::{
        AmbiguityScale, AmbiguitySet, FixedSolveOpts, FloatSolveOpts, MeasModel,
        ResidualValidationOpts, StochasticModel, ValidatedFixedSolveOpts,
    },
    RtkFixedConfig,
};
let epochs = Vec::new();
let ambiguity_ids = Vec::<String>::new();
let ambiguity_satellites = BTreeMap::new();
let wavelengths_m = BTreeMap::new();
let offsets_m = BTreeMap::new();
let float_only_systems = Vec::new();
let ambiguity_set = AmbiguitySet {
    ids: &ambiguity_ids,
    satellites: &ambiguity_satellites,
    scale: AmbiguityScale {
        wavelengths_m: &wavelengths_m,
        offsets_m: &offsets_m,
    },
    float_only_systems: &float_only_systems,
};
let model = MeasModel {
    code_sigma_m: 0.3,
    phase_sigma_m: 0.003,
    sagnac: true,
    stochastic: StochasticModel::Rtklib,
};
let opts = ValidatedFixedSolveOpts {
    float: FloatSolveOpts {
        position_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        ambiguity_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        max_iterations: 1,
    },
    fixed: FixedSolveOpts {
        position_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        ambiguity_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        max_iterations: 1,
        ratio_threshold: 3.0,
        partial_ambiguity_resolution: false,
        partial_min_ambiguities: 4,
    },
    residual: ResidualValidationOpts {
        threshold_sigma: None,
        max_exclusions: 0,
    },
};
let config = RtkFixedConfig::new(&epochs, [0.0; 3], ambiguity_set, &model, opts);
config.with_initial_baseline_m([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]);
let _ = sidereon::solve_rtk_fixed_with(config);
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- Code-differential GNSS (DGPS) pseudorange corrections.

`sidereon_core::geoid`

- GNSS geometry primitives.

- [least_](https://docs.rs/least_squares/index.html)- squares
- Parameter-covariance primitives from the core least-squares substrate.
- [navigation](https://docs.rs/navigation/index.html)
- GNSS navigation-message synthesis and decoding.

# everruns_integrations_docker - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-integrations-docker/0.17.3/everruns_integrations_docker/

## Expand description

Docker Container Integration (Experimental)

This capability provides tools for running and interacting with a Docker container tied to the session lifecycle. The container is lazily started on first tool use and persists for the duration of the session.

Decision: External integration crate, auto-registered via inventory plugin system Decision: Experimental-only (gated behind DeploymentGrade::Dev) Decision: Gated behind FEATURE_DOCKER_CAPABILITY flag (disabled by default on all envs) Decision: Single container per session, named everruns-{session_id} Decision: Lazy start on first tool use, host networking

Configuration (via AgentCapabilityConfig.config):

```
{
  "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/python:3.11",
  "working_dir": "/workspace"  // optional, defaults to /workspace
}
```

# everruns_integrations_deno - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-integrations-deno/0.17.3/everruns_integrations_deno/

## Expand description

Deno Sandbox Integration.

Cloud-based sandboxed code execution via Deno Sandboxes.
Supports multiple sandboxes per session, each identified by `sandbox_id`.

Decision: model the public tool surface after Daytona so agents can switch
between cloud sandboxes with minimal prompt changes.
Decision: BYO connection model — credentials resolve from user connection only;
no env-var fallback. Fail with ConnectionRequired if not configured.
Decision: create sandboxes with a fixed timeout instead of Deno’s default
`session` lifetime because Everruns closes the creator websocket after each tool.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [client](https://docs.rs/client/index.html)
- Deno Sandbox API client.
- [connection](https://docs.rs/connection/index.html)
- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- Deno sandbox session state management.

# everruns_integrations_cursor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-integrations-cursor/0.17.3/everruns_integrations_cursor/

## Expand description

Cursor Cloud Agents integration.

Decision: use Cursor’s public Background/Cloud Agents REST API directly.
Cursor does not publish an official Rust client in the public API docs.
Decision: API key resolves from user connections first, then a per-session
`CURSOR_API_KEY` session secret. The previous process-wide env-var
fallback was removed to enforce per-session credential boundaries.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- Cursor Cloud Agents REST API client.

# sidereon_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#sidereon-core)sidereon-core

The complete Sidereon engine in one crate. It folds the numerical astrodynamics core (orbit propagation, force models, frames, time, SGP4) together with the GNSS domain layer (SP3, broadcast ephemeris, multi-GNSS positioning, RTK/PPP, ionosphere/troposphere, DOP).

- The propagation/astro layer is always present under the `astro`
- The GNSS layer lives behind the default-on `gnss`cargo feature, so a propagation-only consumer can build with`--no-default-features`(plus any astro features it wants) and never compile the IONEX/SP3 parsers.

The GNSS façade is organized by user-facing tasks:

- `ephemeris`
- `rinex`
- `antex`
- `combinations`
- `observables`
- `velocity`
- `positioning`
- `dgnss`
- `quality`
- `observation_qc`
- `signal`
- `ppp_corrections`
- `atmosphere`
- `orbit`

Implementation modules (`sp3`, `rinex_nav`, `spp`, etc.) are crate-private.
This is a clean public surface rather than a compatibility shim around the
original implementation-shaped module layout.

[§](https://docs.rs#units-policy-internal-representation)Units policy (internal representation)

All quantities are stored and computed in **SI base units**, with the frame
and datum encoded in the type name (per the spec’s frames-in-the-type-system
rule), never hidden behind a bare `position_m`:

- **Length / position:**meters (- `_m`). SP3 positions are ITRF/IGS-frame ECEF meters; SPP receiver positions are WGS84/ITRF-compatible ECEF meters. (The- `astro`
- **Time / clock:**seconds (- `_s`). Epochs are represented by the- `astro`- `Instant`/- `TimeScale`), always scale-tagged; there is no bare ambiguous epoch.
- **Velocity:**meters per second (- `_m_s`).
- **Angles:**radians (- `_rad`) internally. Degrees appear only at I/O edges and are named- `_deg`.
- **Frequency:**hertz (- `_hz`).

Field and parameter names carry the unit suffix so the unit is visible at
every call site. Matrix/vector linear algebra uses `nalgebra`
(`DMatrix`/`DVector`) per the spec.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use frame::`- [geodetic_to_itrf](https://docs.rs/frame/fn.geodetic_to_itrf.html);
- `pub use frame::`- [itrf_to_geodetic](https://docs.rs/frame/fn.itrf_to_geodetic.html);
- `pub use frame::`- [FrameValueError](https://docs.rs/frame/enum.FrameValueError.html);
- `pub use frame::`- [ItrfPositionM](https://docs.rs/frame/struct.ItrfPositionM.html);
- `pub use frame::`- [ItrfVelocityMS](https://docs.rs/frame/struct.ItrfVelocityMS.html);
- `pub use frame::`- [Wgs84Geodetic](https://docs.rs/frame/struct.Wgs84Geodetic.html);

# everruns_integrations_browserless - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-integrations-browserless/0.17.3/everruns_integrations_browserless/

## Expand description

Browserless Integration

Cloud browser automation via Browserless REST API and CDP (WebSocket) sessions. Supports screenshots, DOM reading, structured scraping, and multi-step interactions (click, type, keyboard, mouse, touch).

Two modes:

- **REST**(default): Each tool call uses a fresh ephemeral browser. No state, no cleanup.
- **CDP sessions**:- `browserless_open_browser`opens a persistent browser via WebSocket. Subsequent tool calls reuse it (preserving login, cookies, navigation history).- `browserless_close_browser`releases the browser.

Decision: External integration crate, auto-registered via inventory plugin system Decision: REST for one-shot operations, CDP WebSocket for persistent browser sessions Decision: /function endpoint for multi-step interactions (click, type, navigate) Decision: CDP sessions use Browserless.reconnect to keep browser alive between tool calls

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [cdp](https://docs.rs/cdp/index.html)
- Minimal Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) client over WebSocket.
- [client](https://docs.rs/client/index.html)
- Browserless API client.
- [connection](https://docs.rs/connection/index.html)
- [session_](https://docs.rs/session_tools/index.html)- tools
- CDP session management tools: open_browser and close_browser.
- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- Browserless API key resolution, browser session state, and parameter helpers.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [browserless_](https://docs.rs/fn.browserless_api_base.html)- api_ - base
- REST API base URL. Reads `BROWSERLESS_API_BASE`env var with fallback to the default production SFO endpoint. Strips trailing slashes and falls back to the default if the env var is empty.
- [browserless_](https://docs.rs/fn.browserless_ws_base.html)- ws_ - base
- WebSocket base URL. Reads `BROWSERLESS_WS_BASE`env var with fallback to the default production SFO endpoint. Strips trailing slashes and falls back to the default if the env var is empty.

# autometrics 3.0.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/autometrics/3.0.0

Metrics are a powerful and cost-efficient tool for understanding the health and performance of your code in production. But it's hard to decide what metrics to track and even harder to write queries to understand the data.

Autometrics provides a macro that makes it trivial to instrument any function with the most useful metrics: request rate, error rate, and latency. It standardizes these metrics and then generates powerful Prometheus queries based on your function details to help you quickly identify and debug issues in production.

## Benefits

- [✨](https://docs.rs/autometrics/latest/autometrics/attr.autometrics.html)macro adds useful metrics to any function or- `#[autometrics]`- `impl`block, without you thinking about what metrics to collect
- 💡 Generates powerful Prometheus queries to help quickly identify and debug issues in production
- 🔗 Injects links to live Prometheus charts directly into each function's doc comments
- [📊 Grafana dashboards](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-shared#dashboards)work without configuration to visualize the performance of functions &- [SLOs](https://docs.rs/autometrics/latest/autometrics/objectives/index.html)
- 🔍 Correlates your code's version with metrics to help identify commits that introduced errors or latency
- 📏 Standardizes metrics across services and teams to improve debugging
- ⚖️ Function-level metrics provide useful granularity without exploding cardinality
- [⚡ Minimal runtime overhead](https://docs.rs#benchmarks)

## Advanced Features

- [🚨 Define alerts](https://docs.rs/autometrics/latest/autometrics/objectives/index.html)using SLO best practices directly in your source code
- [📍 Attach exemplars](https://docs.rs/autometrics/latest/autometrics/exemplars/index.html)automatically to connect metrics with traces
- [⚙️ Configurable](https://docs.rs/autometrics/latest/autometrics/#metrics-backends)metric collection library (- `opentelemetry`- `prometheus`- `prometheus-client`- `metrics`

See [autometrics.dev](https://docs.autometrics.dev/) for more details on the ideas behind autometrics.

## Example Axum App

Autometrics isn't tied to any web framework, but this shows how you can use the library in an [Axum](https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum) server.

```
use Error;
use ;
use ;
use Ipv4Addr;
use TcpListener;
// Instrument your functions with metrics
pub async
// Export the metrics to Prometheus
pub async
```
## Quickstart

See the [Github repo README](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs#quickstart) to quickly add `autometrics` to your project.

## Contributing

Issues, feature suggestions, and pull requests are very welcome!

If you are interested in getting involved:

- Join the conversation on [Discord](https://discord.gg/9eqGEs56UB)
- Ask questions and share ideas in the [Github Discussions](https://github.com/orgs/autometrics-dev/discussions)
- Take a look at the overall [Autometrics Project Roadmap](https://github.com/orgs/autometrics-dev/projects/1)

# autometrics - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/autometrics/3.0.0/target-redirect/i686-unknown-linux-gnu/autometrics/

## Expand description

Metrics are a powerful and cost-efficient tool for understanding the health and performance of your code in production. But it’s hard to decide what metrics to track and even harder to write queries to understand the data.

Autometrics provides a macro that makes it trivial to instrument any function with the most useful metrics: request rate, error rate, and latency. It standardizes these metrics and then generates powerful Prometheus queries based on your function details to help you quickly identify and debug issues in production.

[§](https://docs.rs#benefits)Benefits

- [✨](https://docs.rs/attr.autometrics.html)macro adds useful metrics to any function or- `#[autometrics]`- `impl`block, without you thinking about what metrics to collect
- 💡 Generates powerful Prometheus queries to help quickly identify and debug issues in production
- 🔗 Injects links to live Prometheus charts directly into each function’s doc comments
- [📊 Grafana dashboards](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-shared#dashboards)work without configuration to visualize the performance of functions &- [SLOs](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html)
- 🔍 Correlates your code’s version with metrics to help identify commits that introduced errors or latency
- 📏 Standardizes metrics across services and teams to improve debugging
- ⚖️ Function-level metrics provide useful granularity without exploding cardinality
- [⚡ Minimal runtime overhead](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs#benchmarks)

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-features)Advanced Features

- [🚨 Define alerts](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html)using SLO best practices directly in your source code
- [📍 Attach exemplars](https://docs.rs/exemplars/index.html)automatically to connect metrics with traces
- [⚙️ Configurable](https://docs.rs#metrics-backends)metric collection library (- `opentelemetry`- `prometheus`- `prometheus-client`- `metrics`

See [autometrics.dev](https://docs.autometrics.dev/) for more details on the ideas behind autometrics.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-axum-app)Example Axum App

Autometrics isn’t tied to any web framework, but this shows how you can use the library in an [Axum](https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum) server.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use autometrics::{autometrics, prometheus_exporter};
use axum::{routing::*, Router};
use std::error::Error;
use std::net::Ipv4Addr;
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
// Instrument your functions with metrics
#[autometrics]
pub async fn create_user() -> Result<(), ()> {
  Ok(())
}
// Export the metrics to Prometheus
#[tokio::main]
pub async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> {
    prometheus_exporter::init();
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/users", post(create_user))
        .route(
            "/metrics",
            get(|| async { prometheus_exporter::encode_http_response() }),
        );
    let listener = TcpListener::bind((Ipv4Addr::from([127, 0, 0, 1]), 0)).await?;
    axum::serve(listener, app).await?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#configuring-autometrics)Configuring Autometrics

Because Autometrics combines a macro and a library, and supports multiple underlying metrics libraries, different settings are configured in different places.

[§](https://docs.rs#autometricssettings)`AutometricsSettings`

See [ settings](https://docs.rs/settings/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#buildrs-file)`build.rs` File

[§](https://docs.rs#including-git-commit-details-in-the-metrics)Including Git commit details in the metrics

Autometrics produces a `build_info` metric and writes queries that make it easy to correlate production issues with the commit or version that may have introduced bugs or latency (see [this blog post](https://fiberplane.com/blog/autometrics-rs-0-4-spot-commits-that-introduce-errors-or-slow-down-your-application) for details).

The `version` label is set automatically based on the version in your crate’s `Cargo.toml` file.

You can set `commit` and `branch` labels using the `AUTOMETRICS_COMMIT` and `AUTOMETRICS_BRANCH` environment variables , or you can use the [ vergen](https://crates.io/crates/vergen) crate to attach them automatically:

`cargo add vergen --features git,gitcl````
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  vergen::EmitBuilder::builder()
      .git_sha(true)
      .git_branch()
      .emit()
      .expect("Unable to generate build info");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-prometheus-url)Custom Prometheus URL

The Autometrics macro inserts Prometheus query links into function documentation. By default, the links point to `http://localhost:9090` but you can configure it to use a custom URL using a compile-time environment variable in your `build.rs` file:

```
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  // Reload Rust analyzer after changing the Prometheus URL to regenerate the links
  let prometheus_url = "https://your-prometheus-url.example";
  println!("cargo:rustc-env=PROMETHEUS_URL={prometheus_url}");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#disabling-documentation-generation)Disabling documentation generation

If you do not want Autometrics to insert Prometheus query links into the function documentation, set the `AUTOMETRICS_DISABLE_DOCS` compile-time environment variable:

```
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  println!("cargo:rustc-env=AUTOMETRICS_DISABLE_DOCS=1");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

[§](https://docs.rs#exporting-metrics)Exporting metrics

- `prometheus-exporter`- exports a Prometheus metrics collector and exporter. This is compatible with any of the- [Metrics backends](https://docs.rs#metrics-backends)and uses- `prometheus-client`by default if none are explicitly selected

[§](https://docs.rs#pushing-metrics)Pushing metrics

Easily push collected metrics to a OpenTelemetry collector and compatible software. Combine one of the transport feature flags together with your runtime feature flag:

**Transport feature flags**:

- `otel-push-exporter-http`- metrics sent over HTTP(s) using- `hyper`
- `otel-push-exporter-grpc`- metrics sent over gRPC using- `tonic`

**Runtime feature flags**:

- `otel-push-exporter-tokio`- tokio
- `otel-push-exporter-tokio-current-thread`- tokio with- `flavor = "current_thread"`
- `otel-push-exporter-async-std`- async-std

If you require more customization than these offered feature flags, enable just
`otel-push-exporter` and follow the [example](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs/tree/main/examples/opentelemetry-push-custom).

[§](https://docs.rs#metrics-backends)Metrics backends

If you are exporting metrics yourself rather than using the

`prometheus-exporter`, you must ensure that you are using the exact same version of the metrics library as`autometrics`(and it must come from`crates.io`rather than git or another source). If not, the autometrics metrics will not appear in your exported metrics.

- `opentelemetry-0_24`- use the- [opentelemetry](https://crates.io/crates/opentelemetry)crate for producing metrics.
- `metrics-0_24`- use the- [metrics](https://crates.io/crates/metrics)crate for producing metrics
- `prometheus-0_14`- use the- [prometheus](https://crates.io/crates/prometheus)crate for producing metrics
- `prometheus-client-0_22`- use the official- [prometheus-client](https://crates.io/crates/prometheus-client)crate for producing metrics

[§](https://docs.rs#exemplars-for-integrating-metrics-with-traces)Exemplars (for integrating metrics with traces)

See the [exemplars module docs](https://docs.rs/autometrics/latest/autometrics/exemplars/index.html) for details about these features. Currently only supported with the `prometheus-client` backend.

- `exemplars-tracing`- extract arbitrary fields from- `tracing::Span`s
- `exemplars-tracing-opentelemetry-0_25`- extract the- `trace_id`and- `span_id`from the- `opentelemetry::Context`, which is attached to- `tracing::Span`s by the- `tracing-opentelemetry`crate

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-objective-values)Custom objective values

By default, Autometrics supports a fixed set of percentiles and latency thresholds for [ objectives](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html). Use these features to enable custom values:

- `custom-objective-latency`- enable this to use custom latency thresholds. Note, however, that the custom latency- **must**match one of the buckets configured for your histogram or the queries, recording rules, and alerts will not work.
- `custom-objective-percentile`- enable this to use custom objective percentiles. Note, however, that using custom percentiles requires generating a different recording and alerting rules file using the CLI + Sloth (see- [here](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs/tree/main/autometrics-cli)).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [exemplars](https://docs.rs/exemplars/index.html)- `exemplars-tracing`or- `exemplars-tracing-opentelemetry`or- `exemplars-tracing-opentelemetry-0_31`
- Connect metrics to traces using exemplars.
- [objectives](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html)
- Create alerts from your function-level metrics using Service-Level Objective (SLO) best practices.
- [otel_](https://docs.rs/otel_push_exporter/index.html)- push_ - exporter - `otel-push-exporter`
- [prometheus_](https://docs.rs/prometheus_exporter/index.html)- exporter - `prometheus-exporter`
- Helper functions for easily collecting and exporting metrics to Prometheus.
- [settings](https://docs.rs/settings/index.html)
- Customize the global settings for Autometrics.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [autometrics](https://docs.rs/attr.autometrics.html)
- A macro that makes it easy to instrument functions with the most useful metrics.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/derive.ResultLabels.html)- Labels
- Customize how types map to the Autometrics `result`label.

# autometrics - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autometrics/3.0.0/autometrics/index.html

## Expand description

Metrics are a powerful and cost-efficient tool for understanding the health and performance of your code in production. But it’s hard to decide what metrics to track and even harder to write queries to understand the data.

Autometrics provides a macro that makes it trivial to instrument any function with the most useful metrics: request rate, error rate, and latency. It standardizes these metrics and then generates powerful Prometheus queries based on your function details to help you quickly identify and debug issues in production.

[§](https://docs.rs#benefits)Benefits

- [✨](https://docs.rs/attr.autometrics.html)macro adds useful metrics to any function or- `#[autometrics]`- `impl`block, without you thinking about what metrics to collect
- 💡 Generates powerful Prometheus queries to help quickly identify and debug issues in production
- 🔗 Injects links to live Prometheus charts directly into each function’s doc comments
- [📊 Grafana dashboards](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-shared#dashboards)work without configuration to visualize the performance of functions &- [SLOs](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html)
- 🔍 Correlates your code’s version with metrics to help identify commits that introduced errors or latency
- 📏 Standardizes metrics across services and teams to improve debugging
- ⚖️ Function-level metrics provide useful granularity without exploding cardinality
- [⚡ Minimal runtime overhead](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs#benchmarks)

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-features)Advanced Features

- [🚨 Define alerts](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html)using SLO best practices directly in your source code
- [📍 Attach exemplars](https://docs.rs/exemplars/index.html)automatically to connect metrics with traces
- [⚙️ Configurable](https://docs.rs#metrics-backends)metric collection library (- `opentelemetry`- `prometheus`- `prometheus-client`- `metrics`

See [autometrics.dev](https://docs.autometrics.dev/) for more details on the ideas behind autometrics.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-axum-app)Example Axum App

Autometrics isn’t tied to any web framework, but this shows how you can use the library in an [Axum](https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum) server.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use autometrics::{autometrics, prometheus_exporter};
use axum::{routing::*, Router};
use std::error::Error;
use std::net::Ipv4Addr;
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
// Instrument your functions with metrics
#[autometrics]
pub async fn create_user() -> Result<(), ()> {
  Ok(())
}
// Export the metrics to Prometheus
#[tokio::main]
pub async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> {
    prometheus_exporter::init();
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/users", post(create_user))
        .route(
            "/metrics",
            get(|| async { prometheus_exporter::encode_http_response() }),
        );
    let listener = TcpListener::bind((Ipv4Addr::from([127, 0, 0, 1]), 0)).await?;
    axum::serve(listener, app).await?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#configuring-autometrics)Configuring Autometrics

Because Autometrics combines a macro and a library, and supports multiple underlying metrics libraries, different settings are configured in different places.

[§](https://docs.rs#autometricssettings)`AutometricsSettings`

See [ settings](https://docs.rs/settings/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#buildrs-file)`build.rs` File

[§](https://docs.rs#including-git-commit-details-in-the-metrics)Including Git commit details in the metrics

Autometrics produces a `build_info` metric and writes queries that make it easy to correlate production issues with the commit or version that may have introduced bugs or latency (see [this blog post](https://fiberplane.com/blog/autometrics-rs-0-4-spot-commits-that-introduce-errors-or-slow-down-your-application) for details).

The `version` label is set automatically based on the version in your crate’s `Cargo.toml` file.

You can set `commit` and `branch` labels using the `AUTOMETRICS_COMMIT` and `AUTOMETRICS_BRANCH` environment variables , or you can use the [ vergen](https://crates.io/crates/vergen) crate to attach them automatically:

`cargo add vergen --features git,gitcl````
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  vergen::EmitBuilder::builder()
      .git_sha(true)
      .git_branch()
      .emit()
      .expect("Unable to generate build info");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-prometheus-url)Custom Prometheus URL

The Autometrics macro inserts Prometheus query links into function documentation. By default, the links point to `http://localhost:9090` but you can configure it to use a custom URL using a compile-time environment variable in your `build.rs` file:

```
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  // Reload Rust analyzer after changing the Prometheus URL to regenerate the links
  let prometheus_url = "https://your-prometheus-url.example";
  println!("cargo:rustc-env=PROMETHEUS_URL={prometheus_url}");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#disabling-documentation-generation)Disabling documentation generation

If you do not want Autometrics to insert Prometheus query links into the function documentation, set the `AUTOMETRICS_DISABLE_DOCS` compile-time environment variable:

```
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  println!("cargo:rustc-env=AUTOMETRICS_DISABLE_DOCS=1");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

[§](https://docs.rs#exporting-metrics)Exporting metrics

- `prometheus-exporter`- exports a Prometheus metrics collector and exporter. This is compatible with any of the- [Metrics backends](https://docs.rs#metrics-backends)and uses- `prometheus-client`by default if none are explicitly selected

[§](https://docs.rs#pushing-metrics)Pushing metrics

Easily push collected metrics to a OpenTelemetry collector and compatible software. Combine one of the transport feature flags together with your runtime feature flag:

**Transport feature flags**:

- `otel-push-exporter-http`- metrics sent over HTTP(s) using- `hyper`
- `otel-push-exporter-grpc`- metrics sent over gRPC using- `tonic`

**Runtime feature flags**:

- `otel-push-exporter-tokio`- tokio
- `otel-push-exporter-tokio-current-thread`- tokio with- `flavor = "current_thread"`
- `otel-push-exporter-async-std`- async-std

If you require more customization than these offered feature flags, enable just
`otel-push-exporter` and follow the [example](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs/tree/main/examples/opentelemetry-push-custom).

[§](https://docs.rs#metrics-backends)Metrics backends

If you are exporting metrics yourself rather than using the

`prometheus-exporter`, you must ensure that you are using the exact same version of the metrics library as`autometrics`(and it must come from`crates.io`rather than git or another source). If not, the autometrics metrics will not appear in your exported metrics.

- `opentelemetry-0_24`- use the- [opentelemetry](https://crates.io/crates/opentelemetry)crate for producing metrics.
- `metrics-0_24`- use the- [metrics](https://crates.io/crates/metrics)crate for producing metrics
- `prometheus-0_14`- use the- [prometheus](https://crates.io/crates/prometheus)crate for producing metrics
- `prometheus-client-0_22`- use the official- [prometheus-client](https://crates.io/crates/prometheus-client)crate for producing metrics

[§](https://docs.rs#exemplars-for-integrating-metrics-with-traces)Exemplars (for integrating metrics with traces)

See the [exemplars module docs](https://docs.rs/autometrics/latest/autometrics/exemplars/index.html) for details about these features. Currently only supported with the `prometheus-client` backend.

- `exemplars-tracing`- extract arbitrary fields from- `tracing::Span`s
- `exemplars-tracing-opentelemetry-0_25`- extract the- `trace_id`and- `span_id`from the- `opentelemetry::Context`, which is attached to- `tracing::Span`s by the- `tracing-opentelemetry`crate

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-objective-values)Custom objective values

By default, Autometrics supports a fixed set of percentiles and latency thresholds for [ objectives](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html). Use these features to enable custom values:

- `custom-objective-latency`- enable this to use custom latency thresholds. Note, however, that the custom latency- **must**match one of the buckets configured for your histogram or the queries, recording rules, and alerts will not work.
- `custom-objective-percentile`- enable this to use custom objective percentiles. Note, however, that using custom percentiles requires generating a different recording and alerting rules file using the CLI + Sloth (see- [here](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs/tree/main/autometrics-cli)).

[26](https://docs.rs#26)///
[27](https://docs.rs#27)/// ## Example
[28](https://docs.rs#28)/// ```
[29](https://docs.rs#29)/// use autometrics::autometrics;
[30](https://docs.rs#30)///
[31](https://docs.rs#31)/// #[autometrics]
[32](https://docs.rs#32)/// pub async fn create_user() {
[33](https://docs.rs#33)///     // Now this function has metrics!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)/// }
[35](https://docs.rs#35)///
[36](https://docs.rs#36)/// struct MyStruct;
[37](https://docs.rs#37)///
[38](https://docs.rs#38)/// #[autometrics]
[39](https://docs.rs#39)/// impl MyStruct {
[40](https://docs.rs#40)///     #[skip_autometrics]
[41](https://docs.rs#41)///     pub fn new() -> Self {
[42](https://docs.rs#42)///        Self
[43](https://docs.rs#43)///     }
[44](https://docs.rs#44)///
[45](https://docs.rs#45)///     fn my_method(&self) {
[46](https://docs.rs#46)///        // This method has metrics too!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)///    }
[48](https://docs.rs#48)/// }
[49](https://docs.rs#49)/// ```
[50](https://docs.rs#50)///
[51](https://docs.rs#51)/// ## Optional Parameters
[52](https://docs.rs#52)///
[53](https://docs.rs#53)/// ### `ok_if` and `error_if`
[54](https://docs.rs#54)///
[55](https://docs.rs#55)/// Example:
[56](https://docs.rs#56)/// ```rust
[57](https://docs.rs#57)/// # use autometrics::autometrics;
[58](https://docs.rs#58)/// #[autometrics(ok_if = Option::is_some)]
[59](https://docs.rs#59)/// pub fn db_load_key(key: &str) -> Option<String> {
[60](https://docs.rs#60)///   None
[61](https://docs.rs#61)/// }
[62](https://docs.rs#62)/// ```
[63](https://docs.rs#63)///
[64](https://docs.rs#64)/// If the function does not return a `Result`, you can use `ok_if` and `error_if` to specify
[65](https://docs.rs#65)/// whether the function call was "successful" or not, as far as the metrics are concerned.
[66](https://docs.rs#66)///
[67](https://docs.rs#67)/// For example, if a function returns an HTTP response, you can use `ok_if` or `error_if` to
[68](https://docs.rs#68)/// add the `result` label based on the status code:
[69](https://docs.rs#69)/// ```rust
[70](https://docs.rs#70)/// # use autometrics::autometrics;
[71](https://docs.rs#71)/// # use http::{Request, Response};
[72](https://docs.rs#72)///
[73](https://docs.rs#73)/// fn is_success<T>(res: &Response<T>) -> bool {
[74](https://docs.rs#74)///     res.status().is_success()
[75](https://docs.rs#75)/// }
[76](https://docs.rs#76)///
[77](https://docs.rs#77)/// #[autometrics(ok_if = is_success)]
[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// pub async fn my_handler(req: Request<()>) -> Response<()> {
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// # Response::new(())
[80](https://docs.rs#80)///     // ...
[81](https://docs.rs#81)/// }
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// ```
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// Note that the function must be callable as `f(&T) -> bool`, where `T` is the return type
[85](https://docs.rs#85)/// of the instrumented function.
[86](https://docs.rs#86)///
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// ### `track_concurrency`
[88](https://docs.rs#88)///
[89](https://docs.rs#89)/// Example:
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// ```rust
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// # use autometrics::autometrics;
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// #[autometrics(track_concurrency)]
[93](https://docs.rs#93)/// pub fn queue_task() { }
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// ```
[95](https://docs.rs#95)///
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// Pass this argument to track the number of concurrent calls to the function (using a gauge).
[97](https://docs.rs#97)/// This may be most useful for top-level functions such as the main HTTP handler that
[98](https://docs.rs#98)/// passes requests off to other functions.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)///
[100](https://docs.rs#100)/// ### `objective`
[101](https://docs.rs#101)///
[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// Example:
[103](https://docs.rs#103)/// ```rust
[104](https://docs.rs#104)/// use autometrics::{autometrics, objectives::*};
[105](https://docs.rs#105)///
[106](https://docs.rs#106)/// const API_SLO: Objective = Objective::new("api")
[107](https://docs.rs#107)///     .success_rate(ObjectivePercentile::P99_9);
[108](https://docs.rs#108)///
[109](https://docs.rs#109)/// #[autometrics(objective = API_SLO)]
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// pub fn handler() {
[111](https://docs.rs#111)///    // ...
[112](https://docs.rs#112)/// }
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// ```
[114](https://docs.rs#114)///
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// Include this function's metrics in the specified [`Objective`].
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// [`Objective`]: crate::objectives::Objective
[118](https://docs.rs#118)pub use autometrics_macros::autometrics;
[119](https://docs.rs#119)
[120](https://docs.rs#120)/// # Customize how types map to the Autometrics `result` label.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)///
[122](https://docs.rs#122)/// The `ResultLabels` derive macro allows you to specify
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// whether the variants of an enum should be considered as errors or
[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// successes from the perspective of the generated metrics.
[125](https://docs.rs#125)///
[126](https://docs.rs#126)/// For example, this would allow you to ignore the client-side HTTP errors (400-499)
[127](https://docs.rs#127)/// from the function's success rate and any Service-Level Objectives (SLOs) it is part of.
[128](https://docs.rs#128)///
[129](https://docs.rs#129)/// Putting such a policy in place would look like this in code:
[130](https://docs.rs#130)///
[131](https://docs.rs#131)/// ```rust,ignore
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// use autometrics::ResultLabels
[133](https://docs.rs#133)///
[134](https://docs.rs#134)/// #[derive(ResultLabels)]
[135](https://docs.rs#135)/// pub enum ServiceError {
[136](https://docs.rs#136)///     // By default, the variant will be inferred by the context,
[137](https://docs.rs#137)///     // so you do not need to decorate every variant.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)///     // - if ServiceError::Database is in an `Err(_)` variant, it will be an "error",
[139](https://docs.rs#139)///     // - if ServiceError::Database is in an `Ok(_)` variant, it will be an "ok",
[140](https://docs.rs#140)///     // - otherwise, no label will be added
[141](https://docs.rs#141)///     Database,
[142](https://docs.rs#142)///     // It is possible to mention it as well of course.
[143](https://docs.rs#143)///     // Only "error" and "ok" are accepted values
[144](https://docs.rs#144)///     //
[145](https://docs.rs#145)///     // Forcing "error" here means that even returning `Ok(ServiceError::Network)`
[146](https://docs.rs#146)///     // from a function will count as an error for autometrics.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)///     #[label(result = "error")]
[148](https://docs.rs#148)///     Network,
[149](https://docs.rs#149)///     // Forcing "ok" here means that even returning `Err(ServiceError::Authentication)`
[150](https://docs.rs#150)///     // from a function will count as a success for autometrics.
[151](https://docs.rs#151)///     #[label(result = "ok")]
[152](https://docs.rs#152)///     Authentication,
[153](https://docs.rs#153)///     #[label(result = "ok")]
[154](https://docs.rs#154)///     Authorization,
[155](https://docs.rs#155)/// }
[156](https://docs.rs#156)///
[157](https://docs.rs#157)/// pub type ServiceResult<T> = Result<T, ServiceError>;
[158](https://docs.rs#158)/// ```
[159](https://docs.rs#159)///
[160](https://docs.rs#160)/// With these types, whenever a function returns a `ServiceResult`, having a
[161](https://docs.rs#161)/// `ServiceError::Authentication` or `Authorization` would _not_ count as a
[162](https://docs.rs#162)/// failure from your handler that should trigger alerts and consume the "error
[163](https://docs.rs#163)/// budget" of the service.
[164](https://docs.rs#164)///
[165](https://docs.rs#165)/// ## Per-function labelling
[166](https://docs.rs#166)///
[167](https://docs.rs#167)/// The `ResultLabels` macro does _not_ have the granularity to behave
[168](https://docs.rs#168)/// differently on different functions: if returning
[169](https://docs.rs#169)/// `ServiceError::Authentication` from `function_a` is "ok", then returning
[170](https://docs.rs#170)/// `ServiceError::Authentication` from `function_b` will be "ok" too.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)///
[172](https://docs.rs#172)/// To work around this, you must use the `ok_if` or `error_if` arguments to the
[173](https://docs.rs#173)/// [autometrics](crate::autometrics) invocation on `function_b`: those

# autometrics in autometrics - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autometrics/3.0.0/autometrics/attr.autometrics.html

`#[autometrics]`## Expand description

A macro that makes it easy to instrument functions with the most useful metrics.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use autometrics::autometrics;
#[autometrics]
pub async fn create_user() {
    // Now this function has metrics!
}
struct MyStruct;
#[autometrics]
impl MyStruct {
    #[skip_autometrics]
    pub fn new() -> Self {
       Self
    }
    fn my_method(&self) {
       // This method has metrics too!
   }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#optional-parameters)Optional Parameters

[§](https://docs.rs#ok_if-and-error_if)`ok_if` and `error_if`

Example:

```
#[autometrics(ok_if = Option::is_some)]
pub fn db_load_key(key: &str) -> Option<String> {
  None
}
```
If the function does not return a `Result`, you can use `ok_if` and `error_if` to specify
whether the function call was “successful” or not, as far as the metrics are concerned.

For example, if a function returns an HTTP response, you can use `ok_if` or `error_if` to
add the `result` label based on the status code:

```
fn is_success<T>(res: &Response<T>) -> bool {
    res.status().is_success()
}
#[autometrics(ok_if = is_success)]
pub async fn my_handler(req: Request<()>) -> Response<()> {
    // ...
}
```
Note that the function must be callable as `f(&T) -> bool`, where `T` is the return type
of the instrumented function.

[§](https://docs.rs#track_concurrency)`track_concurrency`

Example:

```
#[autometrics(track_concurrency)]
pub fn queue_task() { }
```
Pass this argument to track the number of concurrent calls to the function (using a gauge). This may be most useful for top-level functions such as the main HTTP handler that passes requests off to other functions.

[§](https://docs.rs#objective)`objective`

Example:

```
use autometrics::{autometrics, objectives::*};
const API_SLO: Objective = Objective::new("api")
    .success_rate(ObjectivePercentile::P99_9);
#[autometrics(objective = API_SLO)]
pub fn handler() {
   // ...
}
```
Include this function’s metrics in the specified [ Objective](https://docs.rs/objectives/struct.Objective.html).

# autometrics::objectives - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autometrics/3.0.0/autometrics/objectives/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#create-alerts-from-your-function-level-metrics-using-service-level-objective-slo-best-practices)Create alerts from your function-level metrics using Service-Level Objective (SLO) best practices.

Autometrics makes it easy to add Prometheus alerts using Service-Level Objectives (SLOs) to a function or group of functions.

This works using pre-defined [Prometheus alerting rules](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-shared#prometheus-recording--alerting-rules), which can be loaded via the `rule_files` field in your Prometheus configuration. By default, most of the recording rules are dormant. They are enabled by specific metric labels that can be automatically attached by autometrics.

To use autometrics SLOs and alerts, create one or multiple [ Objective](https://docs.rs/struct.Objective.html)s based on the function(s) success rate and/or latency, as shown below. The

`Objective` can be passed as an argument to the `autometrics` macro to include the given function in that objective.Once you’ve added objectives to your code, you can use the [Autometrics Service-Level Objectives(SLO) Dashboard](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-shared#dashboards) to visualize the current status of your objective(s).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use autometrics::autometrics;
use autometrics::objectives::{Objective, ObjectiveLatency, ObjectivePercentile};
const API_SLO: Objective = Objective::new("api")
    .success_rate(ObjectivePercentile::P99_9)
    .latency(ObjectiveLatency::Ms250, ObjectivePercentile::P99);
#[autometrics(objective = API_SLO)]
pub fn api_handler() {
  // ...
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Objective](https://docs.rs/struct.Objective.html)
- A Service-Level Objective (SLO) for a function or group of functions.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Objective](https://docs.rs/enum.ObjectiveLatency.html)- Latency
- The latency threshold, in milliseoncds, for a given objective.
- [Objective](https://docs.rs/enum.ObjectivePercentile.html)- Percentile
- The percentage of requests that must meet the given criteria (success rate or latency).

# autometrics::exemplars - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autometrics/3.0.0/autometrics/exemplars/index.html

**crate features**only.

`exemplars-tracing` or `exemplars-tracing-opentelemetry` or `exemplars-tracing-opentelemetry-0_31`## Expand description

Connect metrics to traces using exemplars.

Exemplars are a newer Prometheus / OpenMetrics / OpenTelemetry feature that allows you to associate specific traces or samples with a given metric. This enables you to investigate what caused metrics to change by looking at individual examples that contributed to the metrics.

Autometrics integrates with tracing libraries to extract details from the current span context and automatically attach them as exemplars to the generated metrics.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-metrics-libraries)Supported metrics libraries

Exemplars are currently only supported with the `prometheus-client` metrics library,
because that is the only one that currently supports producing metrics with exemplars.

[§](https://docs.rs#exposing-metrics-to-prometheus-with-exemplars)Exposing metrics to Prometheus with exemplars

To enable Prometheus to scrape metrics with exemplars you must:

- Run Prometheus with the `--enable-feature=exemplar-storage`
- Export the metrics to Prometheus using the provided `prometheus_exporter::encode_http_response``Content-Type`header to indicate it is using the the OpenMetrics format, rather than the default Prometheus format:

`Content-Type: application/openmetrics-text; version=1.0.0; charset=utf-8`[§](https://docs.rs#tracing-libraries)Tracing libraries

See the [ tracing submodule docs](https://docs.rs/tracing/index.html).

Extract exemplars from the OpenTelemetry Context attached to the current tracing Span.

This works in the following way:

- Add the `tracing_opentelemetry::OpenTelemetryLayer`
- That layer ensures that there is an `opentelemetry::Context``tracing::Span`
- Spans can be manually created or created for every function using the `tracing::instrument`
- Autometrics extracts the `trace_id`and`span_id`from the`Context`and attaches them as exemplars to the generated metrics

See the `exemplars-tracing-opentelemetry` example for usage details.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [tracing](https://docs.rs/tracing/index.html)- `exemplars_tracing`
- Extract fields from `tracing::Span`

# ResultLabels in autometrics - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autometrics/3.0.0/autometrics/derive.ResultLabels.html

```
#[derive(ResultLabels)]
{
    // Attributes available to this derive:
    #[label]
}
```
## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#customize-how-types-map-to-the-autometrics-result-label)Customize how types map to the Autometrics `result` label.

The `ResultLabels` derive macro allows you to specify
whether the variants of an enum should be considered as errors or
successes from the perspective of the generated metrics.

For example, this would allow you to ignore the client-side HTTP errors (400-499) from the function’s success rate and any Service-Level Objectives (SLOs) it is part of.

Putting such a policy in place would look like this in code:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use autometrics::ResultLabels
#[derive(ResultLabels)]
pub enum ServiceError {
    // By default, the variant will be inferred by the context,
    // so you do not need to decorate every variant.
    // - if ServiceError::Database is in an `Err(_)` variant, it will be an "error",
    // - if ServiceError::Database is in an `Ok(_)` variant, it will be an "ok",
    // - otherwise, no label will be added
    Database,
    // It is possible to mention it as well of course.
    // Only "error" and "ok" are accepted values
    //
    // Forcing "error" here means that even returning `Ok(ServiceError::Network)`
    // from a function will count as an error for autometrics.
    #[label(result = "error")]
    Network,
    // Forcing "ok" here means that even returning `Err(ServiceError::Authentication)`
    // from a function will count as a success for autometrics.
    #[label(result = "ok")]
    Authentication,
    #[label(result = "ok")]
    Authorization,
}
pub type ServiceResult<T> = Result<T, ServiceError>;
```
With these types, whenever a function returns a `ServiceResult`, having a
`ServiceError::Authentication` or `Authorization` would *not* count as a
failure from your handler that should trigger alerts and consume the “error
budget” of the service.

[§](https://docs.rs#per-function-labelling)Per-function labelling

The `ResultLabels` macro does *not* have the granularity to behave
differently on different functions: if returning
`ServiceError::Authentication` from `function_a` is “ok”, then returning
`ServiceError::Authentication` from `function_b` will be “ok” too.

To work around this, you must use the `ok_if` or `error_if` arguments to the
[autometrics](https://docs.rs/attr.autometrics.html) invocation on `function_b`: those
directives have priority over the ResultLabels annotations.

---

# autometrics - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autometrics/latest/i686-unknown-linux-gnu/autometrics/

## Expand description

Metrics are a powerful and cost-efficient tool for understanding the health and performance of your code in production. But it’s hard to decide what metrics to track and even harder to write queries to understand the data.

Autometrics provides a macro that makes it trivial to instrument any function with the most useful metrics: request rate, error rate, and latency. It standardizes these metrics and then generates powerful Prometheus queries based on your function details to help you quickly identify and debug issues in production.

[§](https://docs.rs#benefits)Benefits

- [✨](https://docs.rs/attr.autometrics.html)macro adds useful metrics to any function or- `#[autometrics]`- `impl`block, without you thinking about what metrics to collect
- 💡 Generates powerful Prometheus queries to help quickly identify and debug issues in production
- 🔗 Injects links to live Prometheus charts directly into each function’s doc comments
- [📊 Grafana dashboards](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-shared#dashboards)work without configuration to visualize the performance of functions &- [SLOs](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html)
- 🔍 Correlates your code’s version with metrics to help identify commits that introduced errors or latency
- 📏 Standardizes metrics across services and teams to improve debugging
- ⚖️ Function-level metrics provide useful granularity without exploding cardinality
- [⚡ Minimal runtime overhead](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs#benchmarks)

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-features)Advanced Features

- [🚨 Define alerts](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html)using SLO best practices directly in your source code
- [📍 Attach exemplars](https://docs.rs/exemplars/index.html)automatically to connect metrics with traces
- [⚙️ Configurable](https://docs.rs#metrics-backends)metric collection library (- `opentelemetry`- `prometheus`- `prometheus-client`- `metrics`

See [autometrics.dev](https://docs.autometrics.dev/) for more details on the ideas behind autometrics.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-axum-app)Example Axum App

Autometrics isn’t tied to any web framework, but this shows how you can use the library in an [Axum](https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum) server.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use autometrics::{autometrics, prometheus_exporter};
use axum::{routing::*, Router};
use std::error::Error;
use std::net::Ipv4Addr;
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
// Instrument your functions with metrics
#[autometrics]
pub async fn create_user() -> Result<(), ()> {
  Ok(())
}
// Export the metrics to Prometheus
#[tokio::main]
pub async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> {
    prometheus_exporter::init();
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/users", post(create_user))
        .route(
            "/metrics",
            get(|| async { prometheus_exporter::encode_http_response() }),
        );
    let listener = TcpListener::bind((Ipv4Addr::from([127, 0, 0, 1]), 0)).await?;
    axum::serve(listener, app).await?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#configuring-autometrics)Configuring Autometrics

Because Autometrics combines a macro and a library, and supports multiple underlying metrics libraries, different settings are configured in different places.

[§](https://docs.rs#autometricssettings)`AutometricsSettings`

See [ settings](https://docs.rs/settings/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#buildrs-file)`build.rs` File

[§](https://docs.rs#including-git-commit-details-in-the-metrics)Including Git commit details in the metrics

Autometrics produces a `build_info` metric and writes queries that make it easy to correlate production issues with the commit or version that may have introduced bugs or latency (see [this blog post](https://fiberplane.com/blog/autometrics-rs-0-4-spot-commits-that-introduce-errors-or-slow-down-your-application) for details).

The `version` label is set automatically based on the version in your crate’s `Cargo.toml` file.

You can set `commit` and `branch` labels using the `AUTOMETRICS_COMMIT` and `AUTOMETRICS_BRANCH` environment variables , or you can use the [ vergen](https://crates.io/crates/vergen) crate to attach them automatically:

`cargo add vergen --features git,gitcl````
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  vergen::EmitBuilder::builder()
      .git_sha(true)
      .git_branch()
      .emit()
      .expect("Unable to generate build info");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-prometheus-url)Custom Prometheus URL

The Autometrics macro inserts Prometheus query links into function documentation. By default, the links point to `http://localhost:9090` but you can configure it to use a custom URL using a compile-time environment variable in your `build.rs` file:

```
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  // Reload Rust analyzer after changing the Prometheus URL to regenerate the links
  let prometheus_url = "https://your-prometheus-url.example";
  println!("cargo:rustc-env=PROMETHEUS_URL={prometheus_url}");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#disabling-documentation-generation)Disabling documentation generation

If you do not want Autometrics to insert Prometheus query links into the function documentation, set the `AUTOMETRICS_DISABLE_DOCS` compile-time environment variable:

```
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  println!("cargo:rustc-env=AUTOMETRICS_DISABLE_DOCS=1");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

[§](https://docs.rs#exporting-metrics)Exporting metrics

- `prometheus-exporter`- exports a Prometheus metrics collector and exporter. This is compatible with any of the- [Metrics backends](https://docs.rs#metrics-backends)and uses- `prometheus-client`by default if none are explicitly selected

[§](https://docs.rs#pushing-metrics)Pushing metrics

Easily push collected metrics to a OpenTelemetry collector and compatible software. Combine one of the transport feature flags together with your runtime feature flag:

**Transport feature flags**:

- `otel-push-exporter-http`- metrics sent over HTTP(s) using- `hyper`
- `otel-push-exporter-grpc`- metrics sent over gRPC using- `tonic`

**Runtime feature flags**:

- `otel-push-exporter-tokio`- tokio
- `otel-push-exporter-tokio-current-thread`- tokio with- `flavor = "current_thread"`
- `otel-push-exporter-async-std`- async-std

If you require more customization than these offered feature flags, enable just
`otel-push-exporter` and follow the [example](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs/tree/main/examples/opentelemetry-push-custom).

[§](https://docs.rs#metrics-backends)Metrics backends

If you are exporting metrics yourself rather than using the

`prometheus-exporter`, you must ensure that you are using the exact same version of the metrics library as`autometrics`(and it must come from`crates.io`rather than git or another source). If not, the autometrics metrics will not appear in your exported metrics.

- `opentelemetry-0_24`- use the- [opentelemetry](https://crates.io/crates/opentelemetry)crate for producing metrics.
- `metrics-0_24`- use the- [metrics](https://crates.io/crates/metrics)crate for producing metrics
- `prometheus-0_14`- use the- [prometheus](https://crates.io/crates/prometheus)crate for producing metrics
- `prometheus-client-0_22`- use the official- [prometheus-client](https://crates.io/crates/prometheus-client)crate for producing metrics

[§](https://docs.rs#exemplars-for-integrating-metrics-with-traces)Exemplars (for integrating metrics with traces)

See the [exemplars module docs](https://docs.rs/autometrics/latest/autometrics/exemplars/index.html) for details about these features. Currently only supported with the `prometheus-client` backend.

- `exemplars-tracing`- extract arbitrary fields from- `tracing::Span`s
- `exemplars-tracing-opentelemetry-0_25`- extract the- `trace_id`and- `span_id`from the- `opentelemetry::Context`, which is attached to- `tracing::Span`s by the- `tracing-opentelemetry`crate

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-objective-values)Custom objective values

By default, Autometrics supports a fixed set of percentiles and latency thresholds for [ objectives](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html). Use these features to enable custom values:

- `custom-objective-latency`- enable this to use custom latency thresholds. Note, however, that the custom latency- **must**match one of the buckets configured for your histogram or the queries, recording rules, and alerts will not work.
- `custom-objective-percentile`- enable this to use custom objective percentiles. Note, however, that using custom percentiles requires generating a different recording and alerting rules file using the CLI + Sloth (see- [here](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs/tree/main/autometrics-cli)).

# autometrics - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autometrics/latest/autometrics/

## Expand description

Metrics are a powerful and cost-efficient tool for understanding the health and performance of your code in production. But it’s hard to decide what metrics to track and even harder to write queries to understand the data.

Autometrics provides a macro that makes it trivial to instrument any function with the most useful metrics: request rate, error rate, and latency. It standardizes these metrics and then generates powerful Prometheus queries based on your function details to help you quickly identify and debug issues in production.

[§](https://docs.rs#benefits)Benefits

- [✨](https://docs.rs/attr.autometrics.html)macro adds useful metrics to any function or- `#[autometrics]`- `impl`block, without you thinking about what metrics to collect
- 💡 Generates powerful Prometheus queries to help quickly identify and debug issues in production
- 🔗 Injects links to live Prometheus charts directly into each function’s doc comments
- [📊 Grafana dashboards](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-shared#dashboards)work without configuration to visualize the performance of functions &- [SLOs](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html)
- 🔍 Correlates your code’s version with metrics to help identify commits that introduced errors or latency
- 📏 Standardizes metrics across services and teams to improve debugging
- ⚖️ Function-level metrics provide useful granularity without exploding cardinality
- [⚡ Minimal runtime overhead](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs#benchmarks)

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-features)Advanced Features

- [🚨 Define alerts](https://docs.rs/objectives/index.html)using SLO best practices directly in your source code
- [📍 Attach exemplars](https://docs.rs/exemplars/index.html)automatically to connect metrics with traces
- [⚙️ Configurable](https://docs.rs#metrics-backends)metric collection library (- `opentelemetry`- `prometheus`- `prometheus-client`- `metrics`

See [autometrics.dev](https://docs.autometrics.dev/) for more details on the ideas behind autometrics.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-axum-app)Example Axum App

Autometrics isn’t tied to any web framework, but this shows how you can use the library in an [Axum](https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum) server.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use autometrics::{autometrics, prometheus_exporter};
use axum::{routing::*, Router};
use std::error::Error;
use std::net::Ipv4Addr;
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
// Instrument your functions with metrics
#[autometrics]
pub async fn create_user() -> Result<(), ()> {
  Ok(())
}
// Export the metrics to Prometheus
#[tokio::main]
pub async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> {
    prometheus_exporter::init();
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/users", post(create_user))
        .route(
            "/metrics",
            get(|| async { prometheus_exporter::encode_http_response() }),
        );
    let listener = TcpListener::bind((Ipv4Addr::from([127, 0, 0, 1]), 0)).await?;
    axum::serve(listener, app).await?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#configuring-autometrics)Configuring Autometrics

Because Autometrics combines a macro and a library, and supports multiple underlying metrics libraries, different settings are configured in different places.

[§](https://docs.rs#autometricssettings)`AutometricsSettings`

See [ settings](https://docs.rs/settings/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#buildrs-file)`build.rs` File

[§](https://docs.rs#including-git-commit-details-in-the-metrics)Including Git commit details in the metrics

Autometrics produces a `build_info` metric and writes queries that make it easy to correlate production issues with the commit or version that may have introduced bugs or latency (see [this blog post](https://fiberplane.com/blog/autometrics-rs-0-4-spot-commits-that-introduce-errors-or-slow-down-your-application) for details).

The `version` label is set automatically based on the version in your crate’s `Cargo.toml` file.

You can set `commit` and `branch` labels using the `AUTOMETRICS_COMMIT` and `AUTOMETRICS_BRANCH` environment variables , or you can use the [ vergen](https://crates.io/crates/vergen) crate to attach them automatically:

`cargo add vergen --features git,gitcl````
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  vergen::EmitBuilder::builder()
      .git_sha(true)
      .git_branch()
      .emit()
      .expect("Unable to generate build info");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-prometheus-url)Custom Prometheus URL

The Autometrics macro inserts Prometheus query links into function documentation. By default, the links point to `http://localhost:9090` but you can configure it to use a custom URL using a compile-time environment variable in your `build.rs` file:

```
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  // Reload Rust analyzer after changing the Prometheus URL to regenerate the links
  let prometheus_url = "https://your-prometheus-url.example";
  println!("cargo:rustc-env=PROMETHEUS_URL={prometheus_url}");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#disabling-documentation-generation)Disabling documentation generation

If you do not want Autometrics to insert Prometheus query links into the function documentation, set the `AUTOMETRICS_DISABLE_DOCS` compile-time environment variable:

```
// build.rs
pub fn main() {
  println!("cargo:rustc-env=AUTOMETRICS_DISABLE_DOCS=1");
}
```

[§](https://docs.rs#pushing-metrics)Pushing metrics

Easily push collected metrics to a OpenTelemetry collector and compatible software. Combine one of the transport feature flags together with your runtime feature flag:

**Transport feature flags**:

- `otel-push-exporter-http`- metrics sent over HTTP(s) using- `hyper`
- `otel-push-exporter-grpc`- metrics sent over gRPC using- `tonic`

**Runtime feature flags**:

- `otel-push-exporter-tokio`- tokio
- `otel-push-exporter-tokio-current-thread`- tokio with- `flavor = "current_thread"`
- `otel-push-exporter-async-std`- async-std

If you require more customization than these offered feature flags, enable just
`otel-push-exporter` and follow the [example](https://github.com/autometrics-dev/autometrics-rs/tree/main/examples/opentelemetry-push-custom).

# Distributed slice

A distributed slice is a collection of static elements that are gathered into a contiguous section of the binary by the linker. Slice elements may be defined individually from anywhere in the dependency graph of the final binary.

The implementation is based on `link_section` attributes and platform-specific
linker support. It does not involve life-before-main or any other runtime
initialization on any platform. This is a zero-cost safe abstraction that
operates entirely during compilation and linking.

### Declaration

A static distributed slice is declared by writing `#[distributed_slice]` on a
static item whose type is `[T]` for some type `T`.

```
use distributed_slice;
pub static BENCHMARKS: ;
```
### Elements

Slice elements may be registered into a distributed slice by a
`#[distributed_slice(...)]` attribute in which the path to the distributed slice
is given in the parentheses. The initializer is required to be a const
expression.

```
use distributed_slice;
use BENCHMARKS;
static BENCH_DESERIALIZE: fn = bench_deserialize;
```
Elements may be defined in the same crate that declares the distributed slice, or in any downstream crate. Elements across all crates linked into the final binary will be observed to be present in the slice at runtime.

The distributed slice behaves in all ways like `&'static [T]`.

```
```
The compiler will require that the static element type matches with the element type of the distributed slice. If the two do not match, the program will not compile:

```
static BENCH_WTF: usize = 999;
```
```
error[E0308]: mismatched types
  --> src/distributed_slice.rs:65:19
   |
17 | static BENCH_WTF: usize = 999;
   |                   ^^^^^ expected fn pointer, found `usize`
   |
   = note: expected fn pointer `fn(&mut other_crate::Bencher)`
                    found type `usize`
```
### Function elements

As a shorthand for the common case of distributed slices containing function pointers, the distributed_slice attribute may be applied directly to a function definition to place a pointer to that function into a distributed slice.

```
use distributed_slice;
pub static BENCHMARKS: ;
// Equivalent to:
//
//    #[distributed_slice(BENCHMARKS)]
//    static _: fn(&mut Bencher) = bench_deserialize;
//
```

# what's it all about?

**metrics** provides macros, similar to the [ log](https://docs.rs/log) crate, that let library and executable authors instrument their code by collecting metrics -- incrementing counters, gauges, and histograms -- about their code, deferring the collecting and export of these metrics to whatever the installed metrics library is.

# once_cell 1.21.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/once_cell/^1.17

# Overview

`once_cell` provides two new cell-like types, `unsync::OnceCell` and `sync::OnceCell`. `OnceCell`
might store arbitrary non-`Copy` types, can be assigned to at most once and provide direct access
to the stored contents. In a nutshell, API looks *roughly* like this:

```
```
Note that, like with `RefCell` and `Mutex`, the `set` method requires only a shared reference.
Because of the single assignment restriction `get` can return an `&T` instead of `Ref<T>`
or `MutexGuard<T>`.

`once_cell` also has a `Lazy<T>` type, build on top of `OnceCell` which provides the same API as
the `lazy_static!` macro, but without using any macros:

```
use ;
use Lazy;
static GLOBAL_DATA:  = new;
```
More patterns and use-cases are in the [docs](https://docs.rs/once_cell/)!
